comparison: not gradable — softened with *a bit* or *a little too*
form: compound — from the phrase *the devil may care*

senses.gloss: Relaxed and careless about danger, rules or what happens next.
examples: He drove with a *devil-may-care* attitude that scared his passengers.
Her *devil-may-care* charm won everyone over.
His approach to money was a little too *devil-may-care* for his wife.

senses.gloss: Playfully naughty, often in an attractive way.
examples: He gave me a *devilish* grin.
There was a *devilish* twinkle in her eye.

senses.gloss: Evil and cunning, like the devil.
examples: They came up with a *devilish* plan to ruin him.
The villain's schemes grow *more devilish* with every episode.

senses.gloss: Using secret, dishonest tricks to get what you want.
examples: He's too *devious* to trust with the money.
She used *devious* methods to get the promotion.
It was the *most devious* scheme the detective had ever seen.

senses.gloss: Not straight or direct, of a route or path.
examples: The taxi took a *devious* route through the back streets.
The path to the summit was long and *devious*.

position: predicative only — or right after a noun: *a face devoid of emotion*
comparison: not gradable — *completely* or *almost* often go before it
contrast: *Devoid* never stands alone and never goes before a noun: *a room devoid of furniture*, not *a devoid room*. For the everyday idea, say *empty* or *without*.

senses.gloss: Completely without something.
examples: The room was *devoid* of furniture.
His voice was completely *devoid* of emotion.
It's a comedy *devoid* of any real humor.

contrast: *To* here is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing*: *devoted to helping others*, not *devoted to help others*.

senses.gloss: Loving and loyal to someone or something.
examples: She's a *devoted* mother of three.
He was *devoted* to his wife for fifty years.
No fan is *more devoted* than my dad.

senses.gloss: Given over entirely to one subject or purpose.
examples: The museum has a whole floor *devoted* to jazz.
It's a website *devoted* to vintage cars.

senses.gloss: Deeply religious.
examples: Her grandparents were *devout* Catholics.
He grew up in a *devout* Muslim family.
She became *more devout* as she got older.

senses.gloss: Sincere and deeply committed to a cause, team or belief.
examples: He's a *devout* Yankees fan.
She's a *devout* believer in free markets.

senses.gloss: Wet with dew.
examples: We walked barefoot through the *dewy* grass at dawn.
The fields were still *dewy* and cold.

senses.gloss: Of skin, looking fresh, moist and glowing.
examples: This moisturizer gives your face a *dewy* glow.
Her skin looked *dewier* after a week at the beach.

senses.gloss: Skillful with the hands, or clever in handling a situation.
examples: Surgeons need steady, *dexterous* hands.
The pianist's fingers were incredibly *dexterous*.
She was the *most dexterous* negotiator on the team.

contrast: *A diabetic* is also a noun, though many people now prefer *a person with diabetes*.

senses.gloss: Having diabetes.
examples: My father is *diabetic*, so he checks his blood sugar every morning.
The nurse works with *diabetic* children.

senses.gloss: Caused by diabetes or made for people who have it.
examples: He fell into a *diabetic* coma.
The store has a shelf of *diabetic* snacks.

senses.gloss: Extremely evil, cruel or cunning.
examples: The villain has a *diabolical* plan to take over the city.
Police called it a *diabolical* crime.
Each trap in the game is *more diabolical* than the last.

position: both — mostly before a noun; after a verb as *diagnostic of*
takes: *of* + noun, after a verb: *a sign diagnostic of the disease*
contrast: *A diagnostic* is also a noun, especially for computers and cars: *run a diagnostic*.

senses.gloss: Used to find out what illness or problem someone or something has.
examples: The doctor ordered more *diagnostic* tests.
The mechanic ran a *diagnostic* check on the engine.
A high fever alone isn't *diagnostic* of the flu.

contrast: After a verb of action, use the adverb: *cut the sandwich diagonally*, not *cut it diagonal*. *A diagonal* is also a noun, the line itself.

senses.gloss: Going at a slant from one corner or side to the opposite one.
examples: Draw a *diagonal* line from corner to corner.
The street has *diagonal* parking.
The stripes on his tie are *diagonal*.

form: -y from *dice* — as risky as a roll of the dice

senses.gloss: Informal: risky and uncertain.
examples: Things got a little *dicey* when the storm hit.
Lending money to friends is a *dicey* business.
The mountain roads get *dicier* after dark.

senses.gloss: Of living or working conditions, very poor, dirty and harsh, like those in Dickens's novels.
examples: The workers lived in *Dickensian* conditions.
The old orphanage was downright *Dickensian*.

senses.gloss: Like the stories, characters or style of Charles Dickens.
examples: The novel has a *Dickensian* cast of eccentric characters.
It's a *Dickensian* tale of an orphan who makes good.

senses.gloss: Bossy; telling people what to do without listening to them.
examples: Her boss has a *dictatorial* management style.
He grew *more dictatorial* with his kids every year.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or typical of a dictator.
examples: The country lived under *dictatorial* rule for decades.
The general seized *dictatorial* powers.

contrast: Russian *дидактический* is neutral, but English *didactic* about a book, film or speaker usually criticizes it as preachy.

senses.gloss: Of a book, film or speaker, too eager to teach a lesson; preachy.
examples: The film is too *didactic* to be much fun.
His tone became *more didactic* as the lecture went on.

senses.gloss: Intended to teach.
examples: Aesop's fables are *didactic* stories with a moral at the end.
The museum's exhibits are mostly *didactic*.

contrast: Also spelled *diehard*. It is also a noun: *only the die-hards stayed*.

senses.gloss: Loyal to a team, belief or habit and refusing to change.
examples: My uncle is a *die-hard* Cubs fan.
Only the *die-hard* supporters stayed until the end.
*Die-hard* conservatives rejected the deal.

contrast: A false friend: Russian *диетический* means low-fat or light, but *dietary* just means *about what you eat*. Low-calorie food is *diet* food: *diet soda*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the food a person eats.
examples: Do you have any *dietary* restrictions?
She takes a *dietary* supplement every morning.
The guidelines give *dietary* advice for children.

contrast: *A differential* is also a noun: *a pay differential*, or the gear box between a car's wheels.

senses.gloss: Treating people or things differently, or based on a difference.
examples: Women complained of *differential* treatment at work.
The airline uses *differential* pricing for weekends.

senses.gloss: In math, relating to rates of change.
examples: We studied *differential* equations in college.
The course covers *differential* calculus.

contrast: Do not confuse with *different*: *diffident* means shy and unsure of yourself.

senses.gloss: Shy and lacking confidence.
examples: He's a quiet, *diffident* young man.
She was *diffident* about her abilities as a singer.
He seemed *more diffident* in front of his father.

contrast: The adjective ends in /s/ (dih-FYOOS); the verb *to diffuse* ends in /z/ (dih-FYOOZ). Don't mix it up with *defuse* (*defuse a bomb*, *defuse tension*).

senses.gloss: Spread out over a wide area, not concentrated in one place.
examples: The lamp gives off soft, *diffuse* light.
Power in the company is *diffuse*, with no clear leader.

senses.gloss: Of writing or speech, long and unfocused.
examples: The essay was long and *diffuse*.
His argument became *more diffuse* as he went on.

senses.gloss: Of food, easy for the body to digest.
examples: White rice is easily *digestible*.
Cooked vegetables are *more digestible* than raw ones.

senses.gloss: Of information, easy to understand.
examples: She broke the report into *digestible* chunks.
The book makes physics *digestible* for teenagers.

senses.gloss: Relating to digesting food.
examples: The *digestive* system breaks food down into nutrients.
He has had *digestive* problems for years.
Ginger tea can help with *digestive* issues.

contrast: *A digital watch* or *clock* is *электронные часы* in Russian — one that shows numbers instead of hands.

senses.gloss: Using computer technology, where information is stored as numbers.
examples: We switched to *digital* photos years ago.
All the hospital's records are *digital* now.
The newspaper has more *digital* subscribers than print ones.

senses.gloss: Showing information as numbers rather than with hands or a pointer.
examples: I bought a cheap *digital* watch.
The *digital* display shows the temperature outside.

senses.gloss: Calm, serious and deserving respect.
examples: She made a quiet, *dignified* exit.
He remained calm and *dignified* throughout the trial.
Resigning would be a *more dignified* way to end things.

senses.gloss: Of a building or vehicle, old and falling apart from neglect.
examples: They bought a *dilapidated* old farmhouse and fixed it up.
The school building is badly *dilapidated*.
Each house on the street looked *more dilapidated* than the last.

senses.gloss: Working hard and carefully.
examples: She's a *diligent* student who never misses a class.
The police were *diligent* in their search.
You'll need to be *more diligent* about checking your work.

senses.gloss: Of a liquid, made weaker by adding water or another liquid.
examples: Clean the floor with *diluted* bleach.
The juice tasted *diluted*.

senses.gloss: Of an idea or plan, made weaker or less effective.
examples: The final bill was a *diluted* version of the original.
The message gets *more diluted* each time it's passed on.

senses.gloss: Informal and insulting: not intelligent.
examples: He played a lovable but *dim-witted* sidekick.
Don't talk to me like I'm *dim-witted*.
That's the *most dim-witted* idea I've heard all week.

senses.gloss: Having a certain number of dimensions, or relating to size and measurements.
examples: The printer can make *three-dimensional* objects.
Engineers use *dimensional* drawings to show exact sizes.

senses.gloss: Of a character or portrait, complex and realistic, with depth.
examples: The actors turn the villains into fully *dimensional* people.
Her characters are *more dimensional* than in her earlier books.

comparison: not gradable — *greatly* or *much* often go before it

senses.gloss: Made smaller, weaker or less important.
examples: People with *diminished* hearing may need hearing aids.
Her role in the company is much *diminished*.
He felt *diminished* after losing the election.

senses.gloss: Becoming smaller or less.
examples: After a point, extra study time brings *diminishing* returns.
The town has a *diminishing* population.
The team's *diminishing* chances worried the fans.

contrast: *A diminutive* is also a noun, a short or affectionate form of a name: *Bobby is a diminutive of Robert* — Russian *уменьшительно-ласкательное имя*.

senses.gloss: Very small.
examples: The *diminutive* actress stands just under five feet tall.
She was *diminutive* but tough.

senses.gloss: In grammar, showing that something is small or loved.
examples: Russian has many *diminutive* suffixes.
"Doggie" is a *diminutive* form of "dog."

contrast: Say DIN-jee. *Dinghy* (DING-ee), a small boat, is a different word.

senses.gloss: Dark, dirty and depressing, or dull in color from dirt.
examples: They rented a *dingy* little apartment downtown.
The walls were *dingy* and gray.
It was the *dingiest* motel on the highway.

contrast: In American English *dinky* is small and unimpressive; in British English it means small and cute.

senses.gloss: Informal: small and not impressive.
examples: We stayed in a *dinky* motel room by the highway.
The TV was so *dinky* we could barely see it.
That's the *dinkiest* trophy I've ever seen.

position: both — sense 1 before a noun only
contrast: Russian has two words — *дипломатический* (about diplomats) and *дипломатичный* (tactful). English uses *diplomatic* for both.

senses.gloss: Relating to relations between countries.
examples: The two countries restored *diplomatic* relations.
He was traveling on a *diplomatic* passport.

senses.gloss: Tactful; careful not to upset people.
examples: She gave a very *diplomatic* answer.
Try to be *more diplomatic* with the client.
His reply was polite and *diplomatic*.

senses.gloss: Very serious or terrible.
examples: The company is in *dire* financial trouble.
Doctors issued *dire* warnings about the virus.
The situation is *more dire* than we thought.

senses.gloss: Of a need or shortage, extremely urgent.
examples: The refugees are in *dire* need of food.
There's a *dire* shortage of nurses.

contrast: In *fly direct to Chicago* or *call me direct*, *direct* is an adverb (also *directly*). *Direct speech* is Russian *прямая речь*.

senses.gloss: Going straight from one place to another without stopping or turning.
examples: Is there a *direct* flight to Denver?
Take the *most direct* route to the hospital.

senses.gloss: With nothing or no one in between.
examples: Keep the plant out of *direct* sunlight.
The crash was a *direct* result of the storm.
I have no *direct* contact with the CEO.

senses.gloss: Saying clearly what you mean; frank.
examples: She's very *direct* — she'll tell you exactly what she thinks.
Can I be *direct* with you?

senses.gloss: Exact or complete.
examples: That's a *direct* quote from the president.
Her answer was the *direct* opposite of what I expected.

senses.gloss: Relating to direction: showing which way to go, or working in one direction.
examples: A *directional* microphone picks up sound from only one side.
Follow the *directional* signs to the exit.
Use your *directional* signal before you change lanes.

senses.gloss: Without a clear aim or purpose.
examples: He spent his twenties feeling *directionless*.
The team looked *directionless* in the second half.
It's a *directionless* movie with no real plot.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *a dirt-cheap ticket*
form: compound — noun *dirt* + adjective *cheap*; *dirt* means as cheap as dirt
contrast: It is also an adverb: *We bought the house dirt cheap*.

senses.gloss: Informal: extremely cheap.
examples: Gas was *dirt cheap* back then.
We found a *dirt-cheap* apartment near campus.
The tickets were *dirt cheap*, so we bought four.

senses.gloss: Causing a disability or making normal life very difficult.
examples: He suffered a *disabling* injury at work.
Her migraines can be truly *disabling*.
Arthritis is one of the *most disabling* conditions among older adults.

senses.gloss: Putting someone in a worse position; unfavorable.
examples: The deal was *disadvantageous* to small farmers.
They were negotiating from a *disadvantageous* position.
The new rules are even *more disadvantageous* for renters.

contrast: Not the opposite of *affected* (затронутый): *disaffected* people have stopped supporting a leader, party or group.

senses.gloss: No longer loyal to or satisfied with a group, leader or system.
examples: The party is trying to win back *disaffected* voters.
Many young people feel *disaffected* and ignored.
Workers grew *more disaffected* with each round of layoffs.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant.
examples: There was a *disagreeable* smell in the kitchen.
Cleaning the garage is a *disagreeable* job.

senses.gloss: Of a person, unfriendly and bad-tempered.
examples: He's a *disagreeable* old man who yells at kids.
She gets *more disagreeable* when she's tired.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone or something is bad or wrong.
examples: She gave him a *disapproving* look.
His parents were *disapproving* of the marriage.
Her tone grew *more disapproving* as he explained.

senses.gloss: So friendly or honest that it makes people stop feeling angry or suspicious.
examples: He has a *disarming* smile.
Her honesty was *disarming*.
Nothing is *more disarming* than a sincere apology.

senses.gloss: Causing great damage or failing completely.
examples: The movie was a *disastrous* flop.
Cutting the budget would be *disastrous* for schools.
It was the *most disastrous* flood in the state's history.

senses.gloss: Thrown away or no longer used.
examples: The beach was covered in *discarded* bottles.
He builds furniture from *discarded* wood.
*Discarded* scenes from the first film ended up in the sequel.

senses.gloss: Able to be seen, noticed or understood.
examples: There was no *discernible* difference between the two samples.
Her accent was barely *discernible*.
The pattern became *more discernible* over time.

senses.gloss: Having good judgment and taste.
examples: The shop caters to *discerning* customers.
She has a *discerning* eye for art.
Audiences today are *more discerning* than they used to be.

senses.gloss: Relating to punishment for breaking rules.
examples: The officer faces *disciplinary* action.
The school has a strict *disciplinary* policy.
He was called before a *disciplinary* hearing.

senses.gloss: Able to control your behavior and follow rules or a routine.
examples: She's a very *disciplined* runner who trains every day.
You have to be *disciplined* to work from home.
The team played a *more disciplined* game in the second half.

contrast: A playful, informal American word; in formal writing use *confused* or *disoriented*.

senses.gloss: Informal and humorous: confused and a bit disorganized.
examples: I felt totally *discombobulated* after the long flight.
The sudden schedule change left everyone *discombobulated*.
He looked even *more discombobulated* than usual.

form: -ing — what causes the feeling; the person feels *disconcerted*

senses.gloss: Making you feel uneasy, confused or slightly worried.
examples: It's *disconcerting* to hear your own voice on a recording.
He had a *disconcerting* habit of staring at people.
The *most disconcerting* part was the silence.

senses.gloss: No longer connected to a power supply, phone line or network.
examples: The number you have dialed is *disconnected*.
Make sure the power is *disconnected* before you start.

senses.gloss: Cut off from other people or from what is happening.
examples: I felt *disconnected* from my friends after the move.
Politicians seem *more disconnected* from ordinary people than ever.

senses.gloss: Not logically linked together.
examples: The film is a series of *disconnected* scenes.
His speech was a string of *disconnected* thoughts.

senses.gloss: No longer made, sold or offered.
examples: The store is selling *discontinued* models at half price.
That paint color is *discontinued*, so we can't reorder it.
The *discontinued* bus route left many seniors stranded.

form: -ed — how you feel; what causes it is *discouraging*

senses.gloss: Having lost confidence or hope.
examples: Don't get *discouraged* if you fail the first time.
She felt *discouraged* by the poor test results.
By March, I was *more discouraged* than ever.

form: -ing — what causes the feeling; the person feels *discouraged*

senses.gloss: Making you lose confidence or hope.
examples: The early results were *discouraging*.
It's *discouraging* to work so hard for nothing.
This year's sales figures are even *more discouraging*.

senses.gloss: Rude; not polite.
examples: The desk clerk was rude and *discourteous*.
It would be *discourteous* to leave without saying goodbye.
Texting through dinner is *more discourteous* than people think.

comparison: not gradable — *completely* or *thoroughly* often go before it

senses.gloss: No longer believed or respected.
examples: The article was based on a *discredited* theory.
The former mayor is now completely *discredited*.
Voters ignored the *discredited* claims.

contrast: *Discreet* (careful, not drawing attention) and *discrete* (separate) sound exactly the same. The noun of *discreet* is *discretion*.

senses.gloss: Careful about what you say or do, so as not to cause embarrassment or reveal secrets.
examples: Please be *discreet* — nobody else knows yet.
He made a few *discreet* inquiries about her.
Could you be a little *more discreet*?

senses.gloss: Not attracting attention; small and quiet.
examples: She wore *discreet* gold earrings.
There's a *discreet* entrance at the back of the hotel.

contrast: Sounds the same as *discreet* (tactful, not drawing attention). *Discrete* means separate: *discrete units*.

senses.gloss: Separate and distinct from each other.
examples: The course is divided into five *discrete* units.
The two problems are *discrete* and should be handled separately.
Data travels across the network in *discrete* packets.

senses.gloss: Decided by someone's own judgment rather than fixed by rules.
examples: The judge has *discretionary* power in sentencing.
*Discretionary* spending dropped during the recession.
Bonuses here are *discretionary*, not guaranteed.

contrast: *Discriminating* usually praises good taste. For unfair treatment of people, say *discriminatory*.

senses.gloss: Able to judge quality well; having good taste.
examples: The restaurant attracts *discriminating* diners.
She's a *discriminating* reader.
Wine buyers have become *more discriminating*.

contrast: For good taste, the word is *discriminating*, not *discriminatory*.

senses.gloss: Treating a person or group unfairly because of race, sex, age or similar.
examples: The company was sued for *discriminatory* hiring practices.
Critics say the law is *discriminatory* against women.
The new rule is even *more discriminatory* than the old one.

contrast: A false friend: Russian *дискурсивный* means logical, step-by-step reasoning, but everyday English *discursive* means moving from topic to topic.

senses.gloss: Of writing or speech, moving from one subject to another without a clear focus.
examples: His *discursive* lectures often ran over time.
The essay is long and *discursive*.
Her second novel is *more discursive* than the first.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone or something is not worth your respect.
examples: She gave a *disdainful* sniff.
He's *disdainful* of anyone without a college degree.
The critics were even *more disdainful* of the sequel.

comparison: not gradable — *badly* or *severely* often go before it

senses.gloss: Affected by a disease.
examples: The surgeon removed the *diseased* tissue.
Cut off any *diseased* branches.
The old elm trees were *diseased* and had to come down.

senses.gloss: Existing without a body, or coming from someone you cannot see.
examples: A *disembodied* voice came over the loudspeaker.
In the painting, a *disembodied* hand floats in the sky.
Over the phone, his voice sounded strangely *disembodied*.

senses.gloss: No longer believing that something is good or worth doing.
examples: Many voters are *disenchanted* with both parties.
She grew *more disenchanted* with city life every year.
The *disenchanted* fans stopped coming to games.

form: dis- + *enfranchised* — from *franchise*, the right to vote

senses.gloss: Not allowed to vote.
examples: Thousands of *disenfranchised* voters were turned away.
In some states, people with felony convictions are *disenfranchised* for life.

senses.gloss: Feeling powerless and shut out of society.
examples: The program helps *disenfranchised* youth find jobs.
Rural workers feel *disenfranchised* by the new economy.

comparison: not gradable — *badly* often goes before it

senses.gloss: Spoiled in appearance by an injury, disease or damage.
examples: He was left *disfigured* by the fire.
Workers restored the statue's *disfigured* face.
Her hands were badly *disfigured* by arthritis.

contrast: A *disgraced* person has lost people's respect; *disgraceful* behavior is what causes it.

senses.gloss: Having lost respect because of something bad you did.
examples: The *disgraced* senator resigned last week.
He left the company *disgraced* and alone.
The *disgraced* coach later wrote a book about his fall.

senses.gloss: Very bad and shameful.
examples: The way they treated her was *disgraceful*.
It's a *disgraceful* waste of taxpayers' money.
That was the *most disgraceful* performance I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and unhappy, especially because you feel treated unfairly.
examples: A *disgruntled* former employee hacked the system.
Customers are *disgruntled* about the price increase.
Fans grew *more disgruntled* as the losses piled up.

comparison: not gradable — sense 2 often with *thinly* or *barely*
takes: *as* + noun, for what someone or something is made to look like

senses.gloss: Changed in appearance so as not to be recognized.
examples: The thief entered the building *disguised* as a delivery man.
Police used a *disguised* van to watch the house.

senses.gloss: Of a feeling or intention, hidden but still noticeable.
examples: It was a thinly *disguised* attack on his rival.
She listened with barely *disguised* impatience.

form: -ed — how you feel; what causes it is *disheartening*

senses.gloss: Having lost hope or enthusiasm.
examples: Don't be *disheartened* by one bad review.
The *disheartened* players walked off the field in silence.
I was *more disheartened* by his silence than by his words.

form: -ing — what causes the feeling; the person feels *disheartened*

senses.gloss: Making you lose hope or enthusiasm.
examples: It's *disheartening* to see so much trash on the beach.
We got some *disheartening* news from the doctor.
The *most disheartening* part was how little anyone cared.

contrast: American spelling has one *l*: *disheveled*. British English writes *dishevelled*.

senses.gloss: Of a person, hair or clothes, messy and untidy.
examples: He showed up late, tired and *disheveled*.
Her hair was *disheveled* from the wind.
After the red-eye flight, he looked even *more disheveled* than usual.

senses.gloss: Not honest; lying, cheating or stealing.
examples: It would be *dishonest* to pretend I like it.
He was fired for *dishonest* behavior.
Politicians aren't any *more dishonest* than the rest of us.

senses.gloss: Shameful and not deserving respect.
examples: He received a *dishonorable* discharge from the Army.
Lying to your own team is *dishonorable*.
There's nothing *more dishonorable* than betraying a friend.

senses.gloss: Disappointed because something is not as good as you believed.
examples: Many young people are *disillusioned* with politics.
She left teaching tired and *disillusioned*.
The *more disillusioned* voters simply stayed home.

senses.gloss: Not wanting to do something.
examples: I was *disinclined* to believe him.
She seemed *disinclined* to help.
After the meeting, he was even *more disinclined* to sign.

contrast: Nothing to do with *ingenious* (clever): *disingenuous* means pretending to be honest or to know less than you do.

senses.gloss: Not sincere; pretending to be honest or innocent.
examples: It's *disingenuous* to say you didn't know.
Her apology sounded *disingenuous*.
That's the *most disingenuous* excuse I've heard.

senses.gloss: Not well connected, so hard to follow.
examples: The movie felt *disjointed* and hard to follow.
He gave a *disjointed* account of the accident.
The second half of the book is *more disjointed* than the first.

senses.gloss: Of a bone or joint, pushed out of its normal position.
examples: He's out for a month with a *dislocated* shoulder.
The doctor popped my *dislocated* finger back into place.

senses.gloss: Forced away from home or a familiar place, and feeling lost.
examples: The war left millions of *dislocated* families.
Workers felt *dislocated* after the factory moved overseas.

senses.gloss: Not loyal; not supporting your friends, family, country or group.
examples: He was accused of being *disloyal* to the party.
It felt *disloyal* to criticize my own family.
The president fired advisers he saw as *disloyal*.

senses.gloss: Gloomy and depressing.
examples: It was a cold, *dismal* day in February.
The future looked *dismal*.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unsuccessful.
examples: The team had a *dismal* season.
Sales were even *more dismal* than expected.
His test scores were *dismal*.

senses.gloss: Shocked, worried and disappointed.
examples: We were *dismayed* to learn the park had closed.
Fans were *dismayed* by the trade.
No one was *more dismayed* than the coach.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think something is not worth considering.
examples: He was *dismissive* of my concerns.
She waved her hand in a *dismissive* gesture.
The doctor was even *more dismissive* the second time.

senses.gloss: Refusing to do what you are told.
examples: The *disobedient* dog kept jumping on guests.
The kids were tired and *disobedient*.
He's *more disobedient* with his mom than with his dad.

contrast: It ends in *-ly* but is an adjective, not an adverb. *Disorderly conduct* is a legal charge in the US, like Russian *мелкое хулиганство*.

senses.gloss: Untidy and messy.
examples: The papers were piled in a *disorderly* heap.
His desk is always *disorderly*.

senses.gloss: Noisy, rowdy and breaking public order.
examples: He was arrested for *disorderly* conduct.
The crowd grew *more disorderly* as the night went on.

senses.gloss: Badly planned, or not good at planning and keeping things in order.
examples: I'm so *disorganized* — I can never find my keys.
The event was chaotic and *disorganized*.
Their campaign was *more disorganized* than anyone expected.

form: -ed — how you feel; what causes it is *disorienting*
contrast: American English says *disoriented*; British English also uses *disorientated*.

senses.gloss: Confused about where you are, what time it is or what is happening.
examples: She woke up *disoriented* in a hospital bed.
The fog left the hikers *disoriented*.
He seemed *more disoriented* after the second fall.

form: -ing — what causes the feeling; the person feels *disoriented*

senses.gloss: Making you confused about where you are or what is happening.
examples: Flying across several time zones can be *disorienting*.
The hospital's maze of hallways was *disorienting*.
The *most disorienting* part was losing track of the days.

senses.gloss: Criticizing someone or something in a way that shows no respect.
examples: He made *disparaging* remarks about her weight.
The review was openly *disparaging* of the director.
Her comments grew *more disparaging* over time.

contrast: Don't confuse with *desperate* (DES-pur-uht): *disparate* means very different from each other.

senses.gloss: So different from each other that they are hard to compare or combine.
examples: The band mixes *disparate* styles like jazz and punk.
The two groups have very *disparate* goals.
It's hard to unite such *disparate* communities.

senses.gloss: Not influenced by emotion; calm and fair.
examples: We need a *dispassionate* look at the facts.
Judges must remain *dispassionate*.
A *more dispassionate* observer might see it differently.

senses.gloss: Not necessary; easy to do without or replace.
senses.ru: необязательный, без которого можно обойтись, заменимый
examples: In a crisis, some staff are seen as *dispensable*.
Nobody on this team is *dispensable*.
Workers felt *more dispensable* after the robots arrived.
